name: The Constitution of the United States
desc: The supreme law of the United States, ratified in 1788. Establishes three branches of government with separation of powers and a system of checks and balances. All federal government authority flows from this document.

children.name: Legislative Branch
children.desc: Article I branch vested with all legislative powers. Consists of the Senate and House of Representatives. Responsible for making federal law, declaring war, controlling federal spending, and conducting oversight of the executive branch.

children.name: United States Senate
children.desc: Upper chamber of Congress. 100 senators (2 per state), 6-year staggered terms. Confirms presidential nominees, ratifies treaties, tries impeachments.

children.name: Senate Leadership
children.desc: Elected and appointed leadership positions directing the Senate's business.

children.name: President of the Senate (Vice President)
children.desc: Constitutional role; presides over Senate, casts tie-breaking votes.

children.name: President Pro Tempore
children.desc: Presides in VP's absence; traditionally the most senior majority senator.

descriptionOfficial.text: The Senate comprises 100 Members, 2 from each State. Senators are elected to serve for a term of 6 years. There are three classes of Senators, and a new class is elected every 2 years. Senators were originally chosen by the State legislatures. The 17th amendment, which became part of the Constitution in 1913, made their election a function of the people.

ombBudget.rowSelection: every account row OMB files under this unit for the year, on-budget and off-budget together, including the negative offsetting-receipt rows
ombBudget.unitsQuote: Data for budget authority, outlays, offsetting receipts, and governmental receipts are shown in thousands of dollars.
ombBudget.precisionNote: the file data from FY 1995 through FY 2031 represent the Budget amounts multiplied by one thousand to convert the amounts to thousands ; detail below millions is not available.
ombBudget.treasuryQuote: The totals are generally consistent with data published in the Monthly Treasury Statement
ombBudget.treasuryDifferencesQuote: Differences between the Treasury publications and the Budget arise from a small number of reporting and classification corrections made subsequent to the Treasury publications and some conceptual differences between OMB and Treasury reporting.
ombBudget.netQuote: Budget authority and outlay amounts are reported net of any offsetting collections, such as fees, fines, and penalties.
ombBudget.signQuote: Outlays are usually positive values. Offsetting receipts are usually negative values .

children.name: Individual Representative Offices (435)
children.desc: Each of 435 representatives maintains a Washington office and district offices. Structure shown is representative.

children.name: Chief of Staff
children.desc: Manages all office operations and serves as top advisor.

children.name: Deputy Chief of Staff
children.desc: Assists Chief of Staff; often manages D.C. or district operations.

children.name: Legislative Director
children.desc: Directs legislative agenda and manages legislative team.

children.name: Senior Legislative Assistant (×2)
children.desc: Handles major policy areas and committee work.

children.name: Legislative Assistant (×3)
children.desc: Tracks legislation and drafts policy memos in assigned areas.

children.name: Legislative Correspondent
children.desc: Responds to constituent mail on legislative issues.

children.name: Staff Assistant
children.desc: Entry-level; answers phones, manages tours, processes mail.

children.name: Communications Director
children.desc: Manages all press and communications strategy.

children.name: Press Secretary
children.desc: Handles media inquiries and social media.

children.name: District Director
children.desc: Manages all district operations and constituent services.

children.name: Deputy District Director
children.desc: Assists District Director; may oversee specific counties.

children.name: Constituent Services Director
children.desc: Oversees casework team helping constituents with federal agencies.

children.name: Caseworker (×3)
children.desc: Assists constituents with SSA, VA, immigration, and other agency issues.

children.name: Field Representative (×2)
children.desc: Represents the Member at community events in the district.

children.name: Scheduler
children.desc: Manages the Member's calendar and arranges travel.

children.name: House Administrative Offices
children.desc: Non-partisan offices providing administrative, legal, and operational support to the House.

children.name: Clerk of the House
children.desc: Official record keeper; certifies legislation; manages election-related records.

descriptionOfficial.text: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) was created on February 25, 1863 (12 Stat. 665), as a bureau of the Department of the Treasury. descriptionOfficial.text: The National Gallery of Art administers a world-class collection of painting, sculpture, and the graphic arts. The West Building includes European (13th–early 20th century) and American (18th–early 20th century) works. An extensive survey of Italian painting and sculpture, including the only painting by Leonardo da Vinci in the Americas, is on display in the Gallery.

descriptionOfficial.text: Created by an Act of Congress in 1968, the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars is a national, living memorial honoring the legacy of President Woodrow Wilson. The Wilson Center, headquartered in Washington, DC, and supported by both public and private funds, provides a strictly nonpartisan space for scholars and policymakers to interact. By conducting relevant, timely research and promoting dialogue from diverse perspectives, the Center works to address critical current and emerging challenges confronting the United States and the world.

descriptionOfficial.text: The United States Tax Court is a court of record under Article I of the Constitution of the United States (26 U.S.C. 7441). The court was created as the United States Board of Tax Appeals by the Revenue Act of 1924 (43 Stat. 336). The name was changed to the Tax Court of the United States by the Revenue Act of 1942 (56 Stat. 957). The Tax Reform Act of 1969 (83 Stat. 730) established the court under Article I and then changed its name to the United States Tax Court.
